speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, now that your Honour is in the chair I have to rise, in the full house, on a question of privilege which affects every member of parliament. The matter is very serious. We have just heard an honoured guest state that we shall not be slaves of despots and tyrants, and that democracy shall be observed throughout the world.
There are three committees of the whole house. One of them is the committee of the whole, so-called; another is the committee of supply, and the third is the committee of ways and means. The house ignores officially what happens before one of those three committees, and, as I was victimized while one of those committees was sitting, it is my duty, sir, to inform you officially of what occurred 
on Monday while the house was sitting in committee of supply, and when the item for general administration of the senate was before that committee. And I will do so with the feeling that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) recalls the well-known grace of my race.
The question that is of the utmost importance to all members of parliament, jointly and severally, as well as individually, is to know how many times a member of parliament has to withdraw a statement made in the house; and also, sir, if a minister can distort with impunity a statement made by a minister, and then call on the Chair for the withdrawal of a statement which comes from the lips of the minister and not from the mouth of the member who is supposed to withdraw the statement.
There is a well-known rule of the house forbidding members of parliament to impute motives to their colleagues. It will be enough to remind Your Honour of standing order 43, paragraph (1):
No member may speak twice to a question except in explanation of a material part of his speech which may have been misquoted or misunderstood, but then he is not to introduce any new matter, and no debate shall be allowed upon such explanation.
Which means, as you know so well, sir, that provided that parliamentary language is used in a statement made by a member, if that statement is not reported correctly a member has the right to mention to the house what he has said. And how many times do members of parliament rise in this house to correct statements which appear in Hansard, in order to remove any doubt about the way they have expressed themselves on any matter which has come before the house? At page 3345 of Hansard we find the chairman stating that I had used the following words in speaking about the senate:
_ They have completely lost any sense of shame in the senate, and with the exception of two or three-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is rising to a question of privilege in connection with a matter which was dealt with in committee of supply and upon which no report has been made to the house. Therefore the house is not in position to deal with the matter. If the hon. gentleman has any authority to show that he has the right to bring before the house something which was dealt with in committee of supply and there decided, I will listen to it. I know of no authority to permit the hon. gentleman to bring a question of this nature before the

Privilege-Mr. Pouliot
house and ask the house to deal with that which has already been decided in committee of supply.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: It is a most unusual case-

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: That is the reason why I interrupted the hon. gentleman. I know of no procedure to permit this. If the hon. gentleman can submit to me a rule of the house which would enable him on a question of privilege to deal with something already dealt with in committee of supply, I shall be glad to listen to him.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext:
I thank Your Honour for
your question, w'hich I will answer as satisfactorily as possible. The case I refer to is unprecedented in the annals of parliamentary history. There is no case that can be quoted where a minister of the crown has distorted and falsified what has been said by an hon. member.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: The hon. member knows that such language addressed to any hon. member of the house cannot be maintained.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: I know that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: The hon. member will have to withdraw.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: I withdraw, but the word "distorted" was not complained of when I used it in committee and when-[DOT]

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: The hon. member is speaking in the house and I rule that the word "distorted" cannot be used with regard to any hon. member. I ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: I will withdraw anything that is unparliamentary, but I say that the minister put in my mouth things that I .never said. I complain bitterly of this because I have been called to withdraw a statement that I hav'e never made. They were imputed to me. According to the whole parliamentary practice a member of parliament has the right to make a statement and to say exactly what he has to say for the defence of his rights and privileges in the House of Commons.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: I will admit that the hon. member has the right to rise to any question of privilege, but the hon. member well knows that a question of privilege should be taken up at the time the breach of privilege complained of occurs. The hon. gentleman had the right in committee of supply to make his protest with regard to any statement that was made, but there is no question of privilege when he brings before the house a matter which has not been reported to the house and which, therefore, cannot be dealt with.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: If you will permit me, no question of privilege can be taken up in the committee. A point of order can be raised and then reported to the Chair. It was impossible for me to do that at the time because the notes had not been transcribed. I did not have the notes and I could not appeal the ruling to Your Honour so that Your Honour could decide upon it. Your Honour will agree that a question of privilege is similar to a point of order, but a question of privilege cannot be decided by the chairman of any one of the three committees already mentioned. That is one reason. The second reason is that the reporter's notes were not transcribed at the time. The third reason is that a member of parliament has the right to bring up a question of privilege before the house at any time in connection with anything that has happened in any committee. I do not want to use any offensive language; I only want to protest against the manner in which I was victimized on Monday last.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: The hon. member is now making a charge which can only be a reflection upon the Chair when the committee of supply was sitting. He has said that he was victimized. After all, the chairman of the committee of supply would be ruling with regard to order. The hon. gentleman cannot say that he has been victimized.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: I did not say that I was victimized by the Chair; I say I was victimized by one of my colleagues, who happens to be the Minister of National Defence.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: The hon. member is now travelling farther afield. I must rule that there is no question of privilege involved. I have already stated that I have no authority to deal with a matter which was dealt with in committee of supply and not reported to the house, nor has the hon. member been able to quote any authority which would justify a question of privilege at the moment. I am therefore ruling that there is no question of privilege.

subtopic: MR. POULIOT-REFERENCE TO INCIDENT IN DEBATE IN COMMITTEE OF SUPPLY ON MAY 29
speechtext: May I ask Your Honour if I may take it up when the house goes into committee of supply or committee of ways and means?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OP EXTENSION OP SUBSIDY AND DEPRECIATION ALLOWANCE IN RESPECT OP CERTAIN VESSELS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the information
of the house I would like to say that, with a view to assisting further to increase the productive capacity of the Atlantic fishing industry, the government has decided to extend its plan for subsidizing the construction of fishing vessels so as to make subsidy available to draggers and long-line vessels from fifty-five feet upwards in length when built for groups of four or more Atlantic fishermen. Up to the present the subsidy has been payable only on draggers of seventy-two feet or more.
The subsidy on construction of the smaller vessels will be at the same rate as in the case of the larger craft-$165 per gross ton.
The order in council which has been passed extending the application of -the plan also provides that, in computing taxation on income or excess profits, the owners of the vessels may take a special accelerated depreciation allowance up to the whole cost of the depreciable assets in any one year or any group of years within a five-year period from the date of the vessels' registration. This accelerated depreciation will be in lieu of the annual rates of depreciation ordinarily granted under the relevant statutes.
Under another order in council which has been passed the same accelerated depreciation as I have just mentioned will likewise be permitted in the case of all fishing vessels -of the schooner class on the Atlantic coast, no matter what their particular type or types, built subsequent to January 1, 1943, and used entirely for fishing purposes for not less than five years after registration.
During the five-year period the owner of each schooner wishing to claim accelerated depreciation allowance .'.nder this latter order
Fisheries

wall be required to submit to the Minister of Fisheries, not later than the last day of February in each year, a statement showing, to the satisfaction of the minister, that the conditions of the order have been fulfilled. The minister, in turn, will submit the statement to the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue. Failure to submit such a statement, or to comply with other conditions of the order in council, will render a vessel ineligible for special depreciation allowance.

NATIONAL REGISTRATION
speechtext: What procedure is followed to keep the records of the national registration of 1940 up to date in respect to each of the following: (a) changes in address of registrants; (b) marriages of registrants; (c) deaths of registrants; (d) registrations of persons who have attained the age of sixteen or have entered Canada since the general registration of August, 1940, and what were- the respective totals of said address changes, marriages, deaths and new registrations received at the central registry in the year 1943?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: NATIONAL REGISTRATION
speechtext:
National registration
records are kept up to date as far as possible in respect to subjects (a), (b), (c>
and (d) through the following arrangements: *
(a)	Changes of address in most instances are reported to the chief registrar for Canada on printed "Change of Address" one-cent post cards obtainable at any post office in Canada, as provided in the national registration regulations. A considerable number of changes, however, are reported in letters from registrants. As changes are received they are recorded on the master registration cards of the registrants concerned. In the year 1943 the total number of address changes reported was 803,243.
(b)	In accordance with the national registration regulations declaration of marriage forms are available at any post office in Canada. On completion of these forms the postmaster (all postmasters are designated as deputy registrars in the national registration regulations) supplies the wife with a new registration certificate in her married name and forwards the completed form to the chief registrar for Canada. On receipt of the forms at the central registry the name is changed on the master card and the date of her marriage is recorded. The change of conjugal condition and the date thereof is recorded on the husband's master card. The form provides for the reporting of the old and new address of both the husband

and wife, and the master cards are revised accordingly. In the year 1943 the total number of marriages reported was 100,523.
(c>
Through the cooperation of provincial vital statistics officials the central registry is advised of the deaths of registrants. Arrangements have been made whereby the national registration certificates of deceased persons are collected and forwarded to the central registry by funeral directors. In the year 1943 the total number of deaths reported was 64,585.
(d)	Postmasters in their capacity of deputy registrars, register young persons as they attain the age of sixteen, issuing to them national registration certificates. The completed master cards are forwarded by the postmasters to the central registry, where they are incorporated into the records. The registration of persons who have entered Canada since the general registration of August, 1940, and of persons discharged or retired from the armed forces, who were not previously registered, is also performed by the postmasters. In the year 1943 the total number of new registrations received at the central registry was 234,863.

speechtext: Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, $140,009,000.

I do not intend to speak at great length about this matter, but this is something about which members of parliament have no information at all. The Commodity Prices Stabilization corporation is not mentioned in the dominion government telephone directory. If it is, I would like the parliamentary assistant to tell us-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is under the wartime prices and trade board.

They go together? I thank my hon. friend for his information. However, it is all the same thing; it is a branch of the wartime prices and trade board. In the commodity prices stabilization corporation, Mr. H. B. McKinnon is the president and Mr. Noble the vice-president, but I do not see the name of anyone who is bilingual, out of twenty persons. Yesterday in the Ottawa Journal there was a news item that referred to the answer given to the hon. member for York South that 293 dollar-a-year men were serving with the prices board. I have made a check in the telephone book of the names of those who appear here and I find only sixteen French names of persons who presumably are bilingual.
The question of the number of Frenchspeaking or bilingual persons who are employed now in major positions in the war departments has been raised in the legislature of Quebec, and I have waited for a long time to take it up here. I will ask the parliamentary assistant to see to it that members of parliament are given some information about the exact number of high officials, bilingual, in these branches as well as in the Bank of Canada and on the foreign exchange control board, and also a description of the positions they hold. There may be a certain number of stenographers, grades 1 and 2, and perhaps 3, who are bilingual, but they occupy minor positions. When it comes to higher positions it is all a closed territory: Bilingual shall not apply.

I have waited a long time to say this. I had occasion to discuss the matter with some of my colleagues and several English-speaking people outside the House of Commons, and they all agree that the treatment accorded to the bilingual people in this country is something unbelievable, something that has to be remedied. That was said to me in Toronto as well as in Montreal and in London by broadminded people who understand that the bilingual element in the country cannot be put in a reserve and cannot be treated in the way it has been by all the war departments. If the bilingual people in this country, and especially French Canadians in the province of Quebec, do not have fair treatment, it is not due to the majority of the English-speaking people; it is due to the stubbornness of some Englishspeaking ministers who do not act with fairness when the question comes up of employing somebody. The one who gets in has to be a close friend of the one who is in already. They are chums, they are pets, and they practice the same favouritism that was twice bitterly condemned unanimously by a civil service parliamentary committee.
My friend, I would say my young friend, the parliamentary assistant (Mr. Abbott), lives in the province of Quebec. He has friends in that province, he is admired in that province, and I am sure he reciprocates those feelings; but I cannot see why some people in the department are showing such stubbornness-I am glad the minister has come in because I would say this to him-in refusing to employ bilingual people in major positions. It is the same in the department of munitions; it is the same in many branches of the Department of National Defence. This is a war appropriation, and I may say that those who speak French are at times ill-treated by some of these fellows.
I have no charge to make against anyone individually; I wish to defend the rights of those who are bilingual, and who should not be ostracized on that account. It is enough to read the list of the high officials-and by that I mean those who have the right to put their name opposite a telephone number under the wartime prices and trade board. Out of approximately 293 there are only sixteen who are bilingual. Is that reasonable?
The province of Quebec is doing very well when it comes to subscriptions to war loans. It is at the top. The first place to reach its quota was a place in my county. Montreal

War Appropriation-Finance
is doing exceedingly well, and even the small centres do very well, much better than other parts of the country. But when it comes to practical matters, when it comes to being given a chance, the bilingual men, especially from the province of Quebec, find the door closed. I protest most energetically against it and appeal to the good sense of the Minister of Finance. I will tell him that if no correction is made the people will remain of the opinion that it is due to the ministers themselves if the good people of my province have no better chance in the public service.

When this corporation was first appointed I brought to the attention of the house certain principles and facts about this policy which started its infancy in 1941. At that time early in the war things needed more control than they do now, and some stabilization. This vote has gone from $2,000,000 to S120,000,000 last, year, and now it is proposed to make it $140,000,000, although we are near the end of the fifth year of the war. I contended, at that time, and I called it to the attention of the Prime Minister, that the two houses of parliament could broaden out their work and give a branch in another place some real war work such as this which they could consider and report on as is done by the senate at Washington.
The control system has done a good deal of good. There is no doubt about that, particularly at a certain stage of the war. But this stabilization corporation cannot do all the controlling and it is going to defeat the very objects and principles for which it was appointed. I remember Mr. Donald Gordon made a speech in Montreal at the start of this proposal. He said that during the fiscal year they would spend about $2,500,000. I think the Minister of Finance said he did not know exactly what it would be. No doubt he was correct at the time. He did not know what it would be because' it was a problematical proposal. Mr. Gordon then made another speech a month later, in Winnipeg, at Easter I think. This second speech was made at Winnipeg. He said it would spend about $2,500,000. It has gone a long way beyond that. Can any business man tell me that he approves the expenditure of $140,000,000 at a time like this on a proposal such as this?
In the first place they applied the proposal to marmalades, jams, and all that kind of product. They waited so long that there was none of it on the shelves of the large and
small stores to control. They waited so long that it became just a gamble in subsidies and their distribution, a gamble with unforeseen events. They are gambling with production and distribution. ' There are many other instances that I could mention. In the mother country they are getting away from that kind of thing and coming back to the old way of doing business and giving the retail man a chance. I know that some good has come out of this corporation. I admit that, but it has not been applied at the right time and it has not been applied to the commodities to which it should have been applied. You can go along the streets of the cities and see certain small retailers closing up. They have gone into the meat and butter business and a great many other articles of food and vegetables and many other things like this.
I fail to see where we have been given value for our money.
We now have a consumers' league. From what I have seen and what I have learned about it and from what I know about the articles covered by the consumers' league- some of the gentlemen who compose it are teachers from universities, teachers trying to apply business principles and all that kind of thing to many articles with subsidy hand-outs -all they know about it is what they consume themselves.
I believe that protection is necessary at a certain time in the war, but the situation has all changed; and this is out of all proportion. We propose to spend $140,000,000 when we are told we have no money to build houses or practically no money to supply housing or for the care of soldiers, and when the small retailer and the working classes are asking for fuel and housing and all that kind of thing. While all this is going on we are going to take a big gamble in the manner indicated. I admit that there are some good men in this corporation, but some of them have never had any business training. They have never had any training in competitive business. I raised this question when the minister's estimates were up last year and the year before. A return was brought down on Monday and I notice that the control boards have 156 press agents and liaison officers boosting this proposal. Some of them write editorials and some of them prepare just ordinary write-ups in the newspapers. There is a staff of 156 in the department. I have seen pictures in some of the society papers of the gentlemen who compose some of these controls and the value of their work. While
War Appropriation-Finance

I have supported the principle I believe it is catering to the big business man who buys in bulk and to some of the trusts along certain lines. It is not carrying out the functions for which it was set up, to prevent spreads and ensure stabilization, and to try to get the necessities of life to the consumer at reasonable prices. It is administered by a few gentlemen. Some of them doubtless have a great deal of capacity and ability. I believe some of the women's branch of the consumers' league do nothing but travel around the country making speeches at community clubs about the fine men and women in the department.
With regard to the consumers' league I fail to see where we are getting value for the money. I believe the time has come when this matter of this corporation should be dealt with by some committee. At Washington a committee of the Senate considers these things. There they have a duplicate house with ours. They have appointed a committee to inquire into these things. There was a complaint here on Monday about this very thing. I voiced that complaint many times about another branch in another place and the Prime Minister told me in 1941 and 1942 and 1943 that we were going to have a meeting with the other place and try to draft out some way by which those controls could be reviewed by a joint committee and other matters like that.

On Tuesday I asked the parliamentary assistant for a statement with respect to potatoes. Could we have it to-day?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Perhaps I might first give a brief background in connection with the potato subsidy. As the committee will recall, about this time last year the supply situation respecting potatoes in Canada was rather difficult. I recall very vividly that almost every day I was being questioned in the house as to what was being done in connection with the supply of potatoes. As a result of that short supply condition it was decided first to pay a subsidy on imported potatoes. Then, since Canadian new potatoes were beginning to come on the market it was felt it would be unfair to Canadian producers to subsidize imported potatoes, without offering a similar subsidy to the producers of Canadian potatoes. In normal times new potatoes are a luxury product, and when they first come on the market they sell at prices higher than those of old potatoes.
The situation last year was such that it was felt that as new potatoes came on the market they would have to be used, in order to fill current requirements. Consequently the ceiling price of new potatoes established in May, 1943 was fixed at the same rate as for old potatoes. At that time it was announced that a subsidy would be paid on domestically grown potatoes. I shall not go into details with respect to that subsidy. Generally speaking however it was to be at the rate of $3.75 per 100 pounds. Perhaps it would be well to give a little more detail than I had intended.

War Appropriation-Finance
Subsidy was authorized to be paid to persons [DOT]who purchased new potatoes direct from a primary producer or his agent for resale, provided that no subsidy would be paid on new potatoes purchased at prices f.o.b. original shipping point in excess of the following:
(a)	$3.75 per 100 pounds when shipped on or before July 31, 1943;
(b) $3.50 per 100 pounds when shipped between August 1 and 15, 1943, both inclusive.
(c) $3.00 per 100 pounds when shipped between August 16 and 31, 1943, both inclusive.
There was in addition provision for the payment of necessary transportation charges and the allowance for shrinkage equal to five per cent of the maximum wholesale cost as fixed by order 236, which related to the selling price of potatoes. Transportation prices were not recognized in the case of potatoes grown within a radius of fifteen miles of consuming centres. The minimum quantity of new potatoes on which subsidy would be paid is seventy-five pounds.
To ensure that producers would have full opportunity to avail themselves of subsidy arrangements, wide publicity was given through the press, regional offices, wholesale and retail trade and the horticultural council, as respecting the growers and shippers.
The subsidy, as was the case with all these consumer subsidies, was administered by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation. It was an exceedingly difficult subsidy to administer. With hindsight, which is always easier than foresight-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: And much more prevalent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, and much more prevalent-it is possible that another method would have been decided upon to take care of this situation. The chief difficulty, I believe, arose because in August, a period which hon. members will recall, when the subsidy was at the $3.50 rate and the $3 rate-and I know the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton knows a great deal more about this than I do -the price of potatoes dropped very materially. It is evident now that no subsidy would have been necessary in order to get potatoes. But I think the committee should remember this, that at the time the subsidy was decided upon, and at the time the public, the producers and the dealers were told that such subsidy would be paid, the condition which developed was, of course, not known.
The subsidy was payable only under certain conditions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The conditions were fairly well known, and they were the same for everyone. Briefly they were these, that in order to qualify for a subsidy a purchaser must have paid a price not in excess of the figures I have mentioned, namely, $3.75 during one period, $3.50 during another and $3 during a third. The subsidy would cover only the difference between the price he paid, and the wholesale ceiling in the market in which he was selling the potatoes.
In other words, to illustrate, if the wholesale ceiling in the Montreal market was $2.73 -and I think that is what it was in August- and the dealer paid $3 per 100 pounds for his potatoes, the subsidy he would be entitled to receive, leaving aside any question of transportation costs, would be 27 cents. If the market price of potatoes on the Montreal market at about that time should fall to $2.40 he obviously would take a loss on his purchase, because he was entitled only to receive a subsidy down to the ceiling price for that market.

Complaints have been received by the corporation with respect to claims made by a certain dealer. A claim has been made for refunding of the subsidy. I do not know that it is necessary to indicate the name of the claimant.

I wish to call the attention of the minister to some features of these stabilization bonuses, subventions and so on, which now amount to $140,000,000. The minister gave a break-down of the figures and it includes for fruits and vegetables, $4,500,000; for discount on footwear, $1,000,000; for furniture, $500,000; groceries, $2,000,000; gloves-leather, $750,000; lumber, $3,000,000, and so on. The trouble with this policy, as I see it, is that it is sectional.
I have confidence in Mr. Hector McKinnon, whom I have known all my life, and I believe that he is a faithful public servant. But politics in this country being what it is, I suggest that the whole principle of bonuses and subventions is bound to be mixed up in politics. I have seen some of the effects produced by premature announcements made by some ladies and gentlemen of the control and consumer

War Appropriation-Finance
league who go around the district from which I come, predicting subsidies. They discuss many of the articles that are covered in the very break-down that the minister gave. Some of these people appear at some dinner, or some other meeting, perhaps, and they make an announcement which I would regard as being tantamount to a tip-off on what is going to be done. Take jams and jellies, in connection with which an amount of $1,000,000 is mentioned. That bonus, and the distribution of it, had been proposed for some weeks, and afterwards it was found that there were no supplies on the shelves of the retail stores or big stores. It may not be so intended, but in my opinion the whole policy operates indirectly against the small businessman, the retail man, while the larger industries, the departmental stores, are well able to take care of themselves. No doubt they do much good work, but the policy may be of advantage to them.
I cannot understand why, when the proposal was first made, when the policy was first started, it did not take into account one of the most important items so far as the house' holder is concerned. I refer to coal and wood fuel:	I cannot see why this item was not included from the first day of the policy. People have to have a fire in their homes for seven or eight months of the year, and there should be a ceiling and subsidy to aid it. They can do -without some articles of food for a while but they must always have fuel.
There is another matter I would urge upon the minister. I suggest that some part of the fund should have been utilized for building small houses and for materials in connection therewith, for the benefit of the working classes. The government did go into this policy in 1928, and again in 1936, 1937 and 1938, and some $85,000,000 was spent in bonuses through the banks. The government guaranteed repayment of the -money to the banks.
These are two of the main items that should be covered by a stabilization policy of this kind. The growers and shippers also may have a tip-off, I do not know; at any rate I suggest that there is much room for improvement in this matter. This policy should cover necessaries of life for the benefit of the poor people of the country.
Another question I would ask the parliamentary assistant is this. Who audits the business of this corporation? Where is this famous war expenditures committee? Have they control over this $140,000,000? This is a war measure. Has that committee no control over it at all? In a letter he wrote to me some time ago, and which I read in the house, the
auditor general said that he had no control over funds which are in the four corners of the war appropriation bill.
I do not wish to throw cold water on this stabilization scheme, because it has done much good for the consumer, but -they are spending money like water, and I would- point out that on seasonal products the consumer does not get the benefit. I read the market returns for the St. Lawrence market and the markets in the Toronto district and I know there is an increase. Never mind what the index shows; the index is not always correct, at any rate from the point of view of the small people. Take fuel, fuel wood and such things. I believe the proposal was last season that in the larger cities this fund could be used to give seventy-five cents in connection with the hauling of -coal, to provide for expenses to the small retail man who has to go to the waterfront and get coal, put it on a cart and take it through the town when the thermofneter is low and the roads are bad. This is one matter to which attention might very well be given. A deputation came from the municipalities last winter and made representations in connection with this matter, but the seventy-five cents was not allowed. In my opinion, if ever a case was made out it was made out on that occasion by these people who come from -the larger centres of population.
There is a good deal of room for improvement in the administration of the fund and its distribution, because in my opinion it does sometimes savour of politics. It seems -to be sectional. I do not know how people can buy strawberries with the prices charged for them. Take the $3,000,000 in connection with lumber. There is scarcity of material, and boards of education are finding it difficult to get lumber and light steel for the construction of buildings.
I suggest that the corporation should hearken to the handwriting on the wall and do something to help the coal industry, especially the small coal dealers, who should be given a small subsidy for delivery. Something should also be done to help the housing situation by the subsidy principle.

I am sorry that a mix-up occurred in my constituency, and in all fairness to the board I will say that I do not think a certain shipper, because he was a Liberal candidate in the last provincial election, was given a subsidy on that account. I do not think the board knew what side of politics he was on. I do not know that the shipper and the growers who received the subsidy were all to blame. I understand that this particular shipper came to Ottawa in the month of August and was misled by a Mr. REVISED EDITION
War Appropriation-Finance

McEwen of the stabilization, board. He went to Mr. McEwen for instructions in the making out of a claim and that gentleman gave him absolutely a wrong idea. He went home and from that wrong idea induced the growers to give him an invoice that was much higher than the price they received for their potatoes. I do not believe that the shipper was all to blame, but I submit that, in order to clarify the situation, the money should be returned; otherwise the other shippers are being left in an invidious position.
I do not think there is any politics in it here, but when it got to New Brunswick politics came into it. They tried to make out that I did not know anything about these regulations, and they also tried to make out that the other shippers received the subsidy, put it in their pockets and did not pay it to the grower, so that it put the other shippers in a very bad light among the growers. I would like to have the whole situation clarified, because I do not think it will put the board in a very good light if the money is not returned. We want some guarantee that the money will be refunded.
I do not believe that the board can justify prosecutions against these people, but, I repeat, the money should be returned. In the first place the subsidy was wrong. When the pricg of potatoes went down the grower received no subsidy, and when it was up he received the subsidy. That was wrong. With new potatoes that are produced and harvested in July and August the growers get only half a crop and they should have received a bonus or subsidy.
I think the domestic bonus or subsidy should be a floor. I think it is a good idea to encourage the digging of potatoes before they get mature and particularly last year when we had a short supply in June and the first part of July when there were $812,000 paid out in subsidies on imported potatoes from the United States. In my opinion this subsidy was only wasted. There was no justification for any subsidy on imported potatoes from the United States last spring except the first part of June. There were about $100,000 paid out the first part of June. There may have been justification for that up to June 10 last year, but after that you could have bought all the potatoes that came from the United States away below our ceiling price. This subsidy developed into a racket. There were imported into Canada No. 2 potatoes upon which a subsidy was paid. Those potatoes were put into cold storage in Montreal and afterwards exported to the West Indies. At least fifty per cent of the $812,000 was paid out without any justification whatsoever. I think the claims were fraudulent. I want the parliamentary assistant to have the board look into

it. If that is done I think he will find, if he goes to the cities of Montreal and Toronto with a proper investigator, that he will dig out more fraudulent claims than come from New Brunswick.

There is one matter I have been unable to understand, from the statement of the parliamentary assistant. I understand that if a shipper of potatoes had paid a producer, let us say $3, for the potatoes, he could then have collected a subsidy from the government.

Which, if he chose- and some did choose-he could pass back to the producers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
No; the subsidy was to enable the consumer 'to purchase potatoes at the ceiling price. It happened that in May of last year, when this subsidy was decided upon, Canada was practically out of potatoes. The hon. member for Yictoria-Carleton nods

War Appropriation-Finance
his head. He knows the potato situation, as someone has said, probably better than anyone else in the house. The fact is, however, that we were practically out of potatoes in Canada. The price of potatoes in the United States, the only place at that time where we could get them, was high. It was decided that we would have to pay an import subsidy, and it was also necessary, as I said this afternoon, to require the use of new potatoes as soon as they could be secured. I pointed out, too, that under ordinary circumstances new potatoes are a luxury product, and in the early season command a higher price than do the old ones. Under normal circumstances the public always have available the choice between purchasing new and old potatoes. They may purchase old potatoes at the old potato price, or if they wish to have the pleasure of eating new potatoes, they may buy the new ones at a higher price. But because of the short supply conditions last year it was necessary to use all the old potatoes available-and there were practically none -and to accept new potatoes. So that the ceiling price on all potatoes was fixed at the same figure. In order to induce growers to dig their potatoes as early as possible it is my understanding that the subsidy was provided, so that if a dealer purchased at $3.75 in the early part of the season he was obliged to sell those potatoes at the ceiling. And the difference between the ceiling price and what was paid was the amount of the subsidy.

In other words, the consumer was the only concern of the wartime prices and trade board. They were not concerned about the producer at all. It was a consumer subsidy, not a producer subsidy. While these potatoes were being imported from the United States, and a subsidy paid on them, the United States market at that time was away below the ceiling in Canada. Growers adjoining the city of Montreal, and others in Ontario, were advised to hold their potatoes in the ground, while potatoes were being imported from the United States. Then, when the growers near Montreal were ready to dig their potatoes, after holding them two or three weeks in the ground, they found that the city was filled with United States potatoes, and the market had gone down below the ceiling price. So that the growers around the markets of Montreal and Toronto lost money.

speechtext: Well, I am not much interested in the first one, because the parliamentary assistant said it was not much good, anyway. He implied that the second one is the important one, and that the investigation made by Daniels, who was sent from-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport seems to be interested in this, too. I do not know just how he is connected with it. In any event, the parliamentary assistant took a firm and, I thought, a most arbitrary stand this afternoon with respect to the production and tabling of the report from Daniels. I believe the principle involved is one which should not be permitted to pass without strong protest and argument. I say that we have to be very careful in adopting a principle of that kind-and I say it without the slightest desire of doing more than establishing a proper principle. I should like the parliamentary assistant to understand that. I do not raise the point only for the sake of criticism of his department. It may seem at times to the parliamentary assistant, from his position inside the workings of the department, that the suggestions, urgings and pleas made by hon. members in this group to have the workings of the government brought into the open, go farther than the interests of the public might demand. I say to him, however, that if an error has been made during this parliament, then <it is that we have not often enough forced the government to disclose what is going on behind the doors of the various bureaucratic organizations and institutions in Canada. In that regard we, as members of parliament, have a duty to the electorate. Debates in the house of recent date would indicate that many things are being done without even members of parliament having an opportunity of being consulted.
Therefore I ask the parliamentary assistant to give the details in this instance, and to table the report of this Mr. Daniels, who made the investigation; because, if even a small part of the eharges or allegations made by>
the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton is true, then it seems to me the parliamentary assistant is placing a very mild interpretation upon the disclosures made in the report, and in respect of the whole problem concerning this one shipper.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is not what the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton suggested.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton placed the blame upon an official of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation.
Not all of the blame.

Hansard will show. The

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
So far as the situation as now described by the parliamentary assistant is concerned, talcing it even in that position, I think the whole matter now becomes less clarified than ever. The parliamentary assistant has not gone very far in giving us the exact particulars of what actually did occur. I take it that he is still continuing to refuse to table the report. He nods his head, so that I take that to mean that we are not intended to have it at the moment. I am going to ask the parliamentary assistant for some information to which I think we are entitled. If the report is not to be tabled I would ask him to give us the main features of that report.
I want to know and I think the committee is entitled to know, first, what the fundings of Mr. Daniels were with respect to the shipper. Second, I want to know what findings Mr. Daniels made with respect to his interviews with the producers. Third, I want to know what recommendations Mr. Daniels made as to what should be done with the shipper involved, whether he should, be prosecuted or whether there should be an ordinary claim made and how long a time should elapse before the money is paid back to the government. I am anxious to know what recommendations were contained in the report with respect to avoiding a repetition and assuring that there will be no repetition of the situation which now exists and which has been uncovered.
Those are matters which I think are very important. It has been rumoured that the attorney general, who is also the Premier of New Brunswick, came to Ottawa either last
week or this week on this particular mission, to deal with this one particular problem among others. I should like the parliamentary assistant to indicate to the committee whether during the interviews which took place between the attorney general of New Brunswick and his department any question of the prosecution of the parties involved was considered and what decision was arrived at with respect thereto. These questions are important in view of the fact that the report is not being laid on the table. Against that principle I am urging very keenly to-night. I think it is a wrong principle. There should not be such a line of demarcation drawn by the government, and sometimes by boards such as this which in many cases seem to be supra-government authorities. I do not very often become vehement in my protests against what I think are injustices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Fairly often.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
My hon. friend says,
" fairly often," but the parliamentary assistant must expect some severe criticism because, after all, we on the outside looking in have not the opportunities of those on the inside looking out. The result is that we can only inquire, we can only ask and we can only demand. But we have certain rights as members of this house to ask a disclosure by the government of particulars when public funds are involved. If we have not the right to inquire into a matter such as this then we may as well extend this principle right across the whole government expending board.
I am going to ask the parliamentary assistant to reconsider the question of letting us know what happened in this instance. Let us know what the government investigator found. These investigators are paid by the people who send us here as members of parliament, and there should be every opportunity of having an account of this stewardship. That principle should prevail in a democratic country. So that I ask the parliamentary assistant for answers to the questions I have asked. In addition I want to protest vehemently against what I consider to be an abuse of our democratic and parliamentary institutions. I do not like to see this parliament placed in the position where "not in the public interest" is flaunted like a brilliant flag in order to threaten and scare those who would inquire or those who would criticize from time to time. We want the truth. We want a disclosure made in the public interest, and I am asking the parliamentary assistant with as much emphasis as I can summon to my command to see that this principle of democracy shall not be entirely overlooked.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: First on this question of principle, I have not had the experience of my hon. friends in parliamentary matters, but I have always understood, and I believe I am correct, that confidential inter-departmental communications, which of course is what this report is, have always 'been considered as privileged. I am quite sure that that was exactly the stand taken by my hon. friend and the leaders of his party when they were sitting on the right of Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have not sat on the right of Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As I say, my own experience is quite limited, but I am convinced, and it has always been my understanding, that that was a well accepted principle of parliamentary practice, governmental practice, or whatever you want to call it. I would suggest that to produce this confidential interdepartmental report would be creating a very dangerous precedent.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why would it be creating a dangerous precedent? It will be creating a dangerous precedent not to produce it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
If these investigators feel that they cannot make a report in confidence to their superiors, that they cannot make a report which is not liable to be tabled, then the public interest will suffer. My understanding is that that principle has been recognized in government practice for years. I do not think it is even open to argument, and I say that with all diffidence because I am a neophyte in parliamentary procedure. But that is my understanding and it is for that reason that I am not prepared to produce this report. Not that there is anything in it to conceal.
In replying to my hon. friend's requests I shall try to summarize the report along broad lines. Mr. Daniels, who made this investigation, came to the conclusion that the prices which it was understood were paid or contracted to be paid to the growers were not the prices which were actually received and that, consequently, on an analysis of the transactions it was clear that under the regulations the subsidy was not payable. He recommended that under those circumstances, as he was bound to recommend, as any investigator would recommend, that the subsidy had been improperly claimed and paid and should be recovered. A demand has been made on the recipient of the subsidy to pay it back. I indicated this afternoon that if that demand is not complied with I assume the corporation will take the appropriate legal proceedings against the recipient of the subsidy to see that it is paid back. My understanding

is that the recipient of the subsidy is perfectly solvent and able to pay. That is the story as far as the particfular subsidy question is concerned.
My hon. friend referred to the attorney general and premier of New Brunswick being here and looking into this matter. So far as I know he had no interviews with the Department of Finance. I believe he did go to see Mr. McKinnon of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, but I have no personal knowledge as to that. That is about all I can say on this particular subsidy claim.

What I said was that some fault might be attached to Mr. McEwen of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation for giving the shipper a wrong steer. But I do not think for one minute that the officials of the board would advise a man to go out and get false statements from the growers in order to get a subsidy.

I think this might be the appropriate item, Mr. Chairman, on which to speak of subsidies in general, and I should like to say a word or two about the Canadian raw leaf tobacco industry. According to the regulations of the Department of National Revenuefa) "Canadian raw leaf tobacco" means tobacco grown in Canada, in its natural state, not further processed than cured and put up in hands, but does not include Common Canada Twist or scraps, waste, clippings, broken portions of leaf which cannot be tied in hands, stems, or deposits resulting from any process of handling tobacco.
(b) "Raw leaf dealer" means every person who packages Canadian raw leaf tobacco by putting it up in hands and stamping same, or who only stamps such hands, for the purpose of sale for consumption.
This trade affects more particularly, not my own district, but the district of Joliette. The traders and dealers are scattered all over the province of Quebec and in certain sections of New Brunswick and Ontario.
The situation is this. The prices board or the stabilization corporation has allowed the growers to charge ten cents a pound more for their tobacco. I do not argue against that because I think every farmer should get as much as he can in order that he may make a decent living. But when it comes to passing on that price increase from the farmer to the consumer, the raw leaf tobacco dealers were prevented from doing that by the rule that no price ceiling can be broken. The dealers have appealed to the tobacco controller and have established from their books to his satisfaction, admitted in letters from the administrator, that their average profit

War Appropriation-Finance
per pound in years past was not more than two and a half to three cents. Yet this year they will be forced to pay ten cents a pound more to the grower, which will mean that they are bound to stand a loss of seven and a half cents a pound if they carry on in business. As soon as this became evident, the association of tobacco dealers got in touch with the department and interviews were had, at which I was present, where the situation was recognized as being one of hardship for the dealers, but the general principle was invoked and it was stated that nothing could be done. At that time I. inquired of the assistant to the chairman of the prices board if I could, with two or three members of the association, secure an interview with Mr. Donald Gordon, and here is the wire that was sent by Mr. Gordon.
Reference your wire regarding tobacco packers regret it is impossible for me to meet personally all groups who are clamouring for interviews. Our tobacco administrator is David Sim, deputy minister customs and excise. He is fully qualified to deal with problems of tobacco industry and will be glad to arrange for interview upon request.
We arranged for an interview with Mr. Sim. I thought that as a member of parliament I might have received a different answer, but I suppose it is quite in order that members of parliament should be answered in this way by the administrators.
Being a member of parliament does not count.

No, even though we are defending democracy. We got the interview and we established the prices at which the merchandise had been sold in the past. When I say "we", I mean all the people connected with the industiy on whose behalf I was appearing as well as on behalf of many of m3' constituents. Another member of parliament, the hon. member for Joliette, appeared with me. We established to the satisfaction of the officers that our profit on the average was not more than two and a half to three cents a pound and that if we had to pay ten cents more a pound to the growers we would have to stand a loss of seven and a half cents or go out of business. This is the letter sent by the tobacco administrator under date of November 12. The letter is not marked personal or confidential, so that I feel I am at liberty to use it:
This refers to your letter of November 8 and the interview had on November 5 by yourself and delegation on behalf of the independent Canadian raw leaf tobacco dealers. Demand was made for an increase of ten cents per pound in the retail price.
The basis for this demand as set forth in your letter and as enlarged upon on the occasion of your interview has been carefully reviewed
by the writer with the officers mentioned and we have concluded that the considerations involved

The fact that we lose seven and a half cents a pound or go out of business entirely.
-are not such as to warrant a departure from the established policy of this administration, which in effect requires that basic period prices plus new or increased taxes must be maintained.
It is realized that, for the reasons you have outlined, it may be difficult for some of these dealers to continue operating, but this, for the time being, should be regarded as a war emergency measure which must be observed in the interests of the public at large.
As a matter of fact it is difficult for every one of the dealers to continue operating, because none of them can make a profit. It simply means, Mr. Chairman, that they must close down their business and deprive their customers who have been used to taking this merchandise of the opportunity of getting it, or else they must enter the black market. I was convinced, knowing the diplomacy and great intelligence of Mr. Sim, that he had signed this letter, as so many of us do, without being sure of what was in it. A man of his diplomacy would never have written that last sentence. The letter must have been drafted for him to sign. It simply means, as I said before, that the dealers must operate at a loss, close their doors or enter the black market. There was a market for hundreds of thousands of pounds of this raw leaf tobacco in the section of the country that I mentioned a moment ago. I got in touch further with the administrator, trying to convince him that a number of the dealers would have to close their doors or enter the black market. The department has some prosecutions pending now of people who have done just that. Dealers found clients willing to pay ten cents a pound more, which they could not pay legally, so that people have been doing it illegally. They have infringed the law, and a number of prosecutions are pending. Those dealers who want to stay within the law did not purchase their stock of tobacco this year because they would have had to pay more for it than their selling price, and many others are in the black market and are ready to plead guilty. Later on I spoke to the administrator over the telephone and we had a long discussion. He wrote me in a letter, which is also not marked private or confidential, as follows:
As I understand the problem, these people find themselves squeezed between the higher price being demanded by the farmer for his tobacco, and the price ceiling which does not permit them to increase their selling price to the public.
T'he proposition put to us was either subsidy or an increase in the consumer selling price. Subsidies have been paid in the case of certain necessary food products such as milk, butter, canned vegetables, also wood fuel, etc., but I

War Appropriation-Finance
am not aware of subsidies being paid to Canadian producers of commodities which were not regarded as absolutely essential.
When I in effect told, you this on the telephone you immediately suggested that in that event if they were to be regarded as luxuries a price increase should be permitted. This immediately raises the question as to whether or not the price ceiling is to be over all in character or selective.
He goes on to say that a further interview will be arranged. Some time in December I wrote the administrator again, stating:
I wish to impress further upon you the importance of the question we discussed over the telephone and I doubt very much that sending one officer of the prices section of the wartime prices and trade board and basing the conclusions of the board merely on that investigation would give justice to the seriousness of this situation. I think that, before putting these people out of business entirely, it would be only just and fair to allow them to put a formal brief before the board and allow them to be heard before responsible parties sitting on the board.
I thought that before you closed down or clamped down on people and forced them out of business, the least you could do would be to have them heard directly by the people responsible for the decision, the board itself. Finally, in February, I received a letter from the administrator:
I have not forgotten your representations in connection with the tobacco packers of Canadian raw leaf, who are squeezed-[DOT]
Those are not only my words, but the words of the administrator.

between the increased price paid to the primary producer and the price ceiling.
He admits the difference in price and the fact that they would have to close their doors. The letter continues:
This week I had some conversations with senior executive officers of the wartime prices and trade board . . . with a view to arranging some solution.
That was in February. We are now in May. No decision has yet been handed down, and all these prosecutions are awaiting the final decision. Many of these people are guilty; others have closed their doors, and there is a "black market", if we can consider as a black market a violation of ceiling price. I think it might be well for the wartime prices and trade board to ponder the advisability of closing a trade entirely just for the sake of maintaining a ceiling, or of recognizing the fact that by doing so they are depriving an element of the population of goods which they are entitled to buy as much as any other people. They do not like cigarettes; they do not like cigars. I do not myself smoke their tobacco, but we are living in a democracy, and they want that kind of tobacco, so why

cannot, we supply it to them when there is plenty of it and it is only a question of adjustment of price? I am not complaining about farmers increasing their prices. Having waited so long before getting proper remuneration, if they can get more now, good and well. The price should be raised in view of the fact that the public would be willing to pay it, and there is the demand. Therefore I think this is quite an opportune moment to ask the parliamentary assistant if he would not consider that question. If he knows about it, would he be ready to tell us to-night if a decision is about to be rendered? If so, I should like to impress upon him the advisability of giving that rise in the ceiling price; otherwise he is closing the doors of one of the important industries in the province of Quebec and he is depriving a number of people of goods to which they are entitled.

Mr. Chairman, in many cases the wartime prices and trade board is far from giving a fair deal to the people in this country. For instance, unaccountable delays occur in the announcement of certain decisions taken in connection with articles that are essential to agriculture. Permits for the purchase of farm machinery, such as tractors, are only issued after weeks and months have elapsed. Once the farmer has obtained his permit, he has to wait even longer for the delivery of farm implements. The restrictions placed by the government on the manufacture of farm- machinery should be lifted at once. They should never have been imposed. Agriculture is essential from the standpoint of food supplies for the army and the civilian population. All those restrictions interfere with production. At a time when more than 400,000 men and women have left farms to take up work in war plants or join the army, is it fair that agriculture should thus be deprived of indispensable implements? Let us be more sensible and practical. I know farmers who, on account of ill health and through the lack of help, will have to leave their farms untilled, because all kinds of restrictions have been placed on agricultural implements and their replacement parts. I urge the government to remedy once for all such a dire situation. Let them take action at once, with a view to amending the legislation whereby the wartime prices and trade board was established.
I shall make one more remark before concluding. The companies which manufacture farm implements should not take the place of farmers in the matter of filing applications with the Board. The government should pre-

War Appropriation-Finance
vent delays in the delivery of farm machinery, such delays often being caused by the companies themselves. In fact, it often happens that the companies file the farmers' applications with the board only after several weeks. Some may ask what their purpose is. I do not know. But I am sure of one thing and it is that discrimination has something to do with that hide-and-seek game. Let the farmers be empowered to deal directly with the Wartime Prices and Trade Board, without having to go to the companies or their agents. If such an infringement of the law and regulations is to be perpetuated, the government had better abolish all those boards and that irresponsible bureaucracy. Finally, it was certainly not worth while to establish those bodies, which become a public nuisance as soon as they interfere with agricultural production in these troublous times.
As far as I am concerned, I can well afford to make these few remarks. Some may voice complaints about that baneful bureaucracy in the creation of which they have had a part. I, for one, have condemned it from the beginning and I voted against its establishment. I believe that was the best course to follow.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I should like to reply at once to my hon. friend, who will forgive me if I speak in English, but I can do a little better in that language than in his. He has complained about the conditions of the issue of permits for tractors and farm implements and has urged that the restrictions on the manufacture of this particular type of machinery should be completely removed.
In that connection I can give the committee a short summary of what the position is with respect to farm machinery. By agreement with the United States authorities and ourselves, the supply of farm machinery and equipment available in each country is on an equal basis and similar rationing plans are in effect in both countries. Because of a shortage of steel and other components, the supplies available during the 1942-43 production year, which ended the 30th June, 1943, were very much restricted; only thirty-five per cent of the corresponding 1940 period taking into account finished machines only, or fifty-six per cent including repairs. That position improved in the 1943-44 period, and it has been possible to increase production substantially, to something over eighty per cent of the 1940 period in terms of finished machines plus 156 per cent of the 1940-41 average of repair parts. The 1944^5 programme, which will end on June 30, 1945, calls for a still further in-
100-217 .
crease, to approximately 100 per cent of the 1940-41 average of completed machines and attachments, with no limit on the production and importation of repair parts. Incidentally, a special production allocation has been programmed for veterans' rehabilitation. The supply situation has eased so far as some materials are concerned, but shortage of manpower has led to difficulty in obtaining adequate supplies of steel sheets, malleable castings, ball and roller bearings and motors. Despite increased production, rationing still continues to be necessary since supplies of many types of farm machinery and equipment are not adequate to meet the demand. Rationing does not apply to attachments and repair parts or to certain lines of farm machinery such as pulpers, hay forks, watering equipment, et cetera. Under the rationing programme each area is assigned quotas of the various types of farm machinery and equipment on the basis of sales in past periods.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: A few moments ago members were discussing alleged wrong payments by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation in connection with potatoes. In that regard I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant some questions relating to another phase of the corporation's work. The subject is the manufacture of bedding, mattresses and general products that are turned out by upholsterers and bedding manufacturers. I understand that one of the functions of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation is to provide subsidies to some of these manufacturers, where necessary, to enable them to purchase first-class material to make the necessary supplies along this line. I would ask the parliamentary assistant to give us any figures he can as to the number of companies which have been receiving these subsidies and to inform us whether any of these companies have returned either voluntarily or involuntarily any portion of the subsidies. In other words, has there been any recovery by the corporation of subsidies paid to bedding manufacturers on the ground that they were wrongly paid? Perhaps the parliamentary assistant would care to answer this question now? I have some others to ask.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It might be easier to answer them one by one. First of all, we would not have information as to the number of firms to which subsidies for this particular purpose had been paid. We would have information as to the amount of subsidies paid on particular raw material going into bedding. The record would be on a financial basis and would relate to tariff items, and I should think probably it would be raw cotton or some textile fabric which would be the

War Appropriation-Finance

type of raw material going into the articles to which my hon. friend has referred. I could give the gross amount paid in subsidy on that particular type of raw material, but that would include similar material for other purposes. I do not think we could segregate it into material going into bedding, for example.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Can the parliamentary assistant tell me whether any firms have been called upon to pay back to the corporation funds received by way of subsidy to enable them to purchase material for bedding? If so, I should like to know what the reason was that the money was recovered?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the first place, claims are carefully scrutinized before the subsidy is paid; but claims for subsidies, and subsidies, are constantly under review. They are investigated, and a claim for refund made if it is found, for instance, that a subsidy is unnecessary and that the recipient can absorb the cost and does not need the subsidy. But I am not in a position to say, and the officials tell me that they cannot say now, whether, for instance, a bedding manufacturer who had received a subsidy on raw cotton or something of that sort used in bedding had to pay back a subsidy paid because he did not need it. The records would not give a break-down in that detail.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: If the parliamentary assistant has not the specific information with the figures before him, can he tell me whether in general any of this recoveiy of money paid in subsidies was owing to discoveries by inspectors that firms had not used the material specified in their contracts or in the claims or in the agreements between the company and the corporation? Is there anything here similar to the situation in connection with potatoes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is pointed out that if we discover that the recipient of a subsidy has violated ceiling prices demand for refund is *made. The subsidies are paid not to guarantee profits but to enable ceiling prices to be maintained, and if it is found, as has been found in some cases, that recipients have violated ceiling prices with respect to goods on which subsidies are paid and the material has been used, a demand is made for a return of subsidies and the cases are reported to the enforcement division of the board.

speechtext:
Have demands been
made for recovery on the ground that the bedding manufacturer has not used the specified proportion of new material? In other words, have there been discoveries that manufacturers have been using second-hand or

used material in the making of mattresses, contrary to the specifications on which they were supposed to be working? Is there any prosecution of such a nature pending at the present time?

I shall have to get that
information. If my hon. friend will allow the question to stand I will get the information later.
