No one has been more critical than I of certain aspects of the wartime prices and trade board, but I rise now to express my praise of the great number of citizens who are operating under the board and who have not been mentioned in this entire debate. I speak of the great work done by the hundreds of men and women who haVe taken in charge the distribution of the ration cards. Throughout the country, municipal councils have provided for this work, and I know that in the city from which I come-and other cities have a similar system-the people there and in the district surrounding are looked after in the matter of ration cards at a cost of only $60 a month. On this occasion I wish to give this word of praise to those men and women who have volunteered to do this work. They have gone to these offices day and night without hope of reward, merely from a sense of service to the country, and have given their services free in turning over these books to the general public. While criticism *may be coming to members higher up in the board, this is one group of individuals working under the board, who, as I think every hon. member will gladly agree, deserve every praise that can be given them.

This credit of $140,000,000 to
the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, which is closely connected with the wartime prices and trade board, is to provide, if my understanding is correct, a subsidy to those who, where the ceiling is too low, suffer losses. It is to take care of losses to producers.
Before the opening of the lobster fishing season in 1942 a ceiling price was placed upon lobsters which was quite low. The fishermen and cooperatives were obliged to sell all their lobster production to the wholesale dealers in Halifax at the price ceiling. After the fishing season was over, the ceiling was removed, and those wholesale dealers who had bought the

War Appropriation-Finance
lobsters from the fishermen at a very low price were allowed to sell them at the highest price they could get for them. Last year we had no ceiling price on lobsters. This spring before the season commenced the ceiling price was again placed on lobsters, which means that the fishermen will suffer a loss of practically S8 a case on their fish. There will be that much difference in the price they will get this year as compared with what they got last year. I should like to know from the parliamentary assistant what can be done to correct that injustice to the lobster fishermen. I believe that the ceiling price should be removed immediately so that the fishermen will not suffer and that the wholesalers will not benefit as they did in 1942. If that is not done the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation should pay a subsidy to the lobster fishermen to compensate them for their losses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Before I reply to the hon. member for Gaspe I should like to deal with the inquiry of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, but before I do that I wish to join with the hon. member for New Westminster in the tribute he paid to those people who volunteered their services in the distribution of ration books. I concur-and I know the minister does-in the views which my hon. friend expressed as to the splendid work that has been done by those volunteer workers. It was a difficult task and they did it splendidly. I join with him in an endorsation of that work.
As to the inquiry of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I am advised that there is no record of any case in which a subsidy has been reclaimed because of the use of second-hand material. Subsidies have been reclaimed where ceilings were broken and where there has been a degradation of goods by using second-hand material and in some cases where goods had been manufactured for munitions and supply which, of course, are not subject to subsidy payments. In one case in which a subsidy was reclaimed on one of these grounds-I am not sure which-the investigation by the corporation also disclosed certain other irregularities which had nothing to do with the subsidy payments. I am advised that those irregularities were reported to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for appropriate action, but they had nothing to do with the question of subsidy payments made to that particular firm.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I take it that the parliamentary assistant was not familiar with the situation before he consulted his officials. In the statement he made he first of all stated categorically that no recoveries of subsidies
were claimed on the grounds I mentioned. In his subsequent remarks he did admit that there was a degradation of quality.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Not in the case of a particular firm. I was speaking generally when I said that subsidies were recovered in two or three instances, first, where there had been a breach of the ceiling price; second, where there had been a degradation of quality below the quality the goods were supposed to be for which the subsidy was given, due, among other things, to the use of second-hand goods; third, where a subsidy had been claimed with respect to merchandise supplied to a government department, war materials to munitions and supply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Just that much of an admission confirms my suspicion and prompts me to question the parliamentary assistant further. He realizes that this is a pretty serious situation, not only with respect to the money involved but with respect to the injurious results to the health of people that could come from the manufacture of bedding which is supposedly brand new and which turns out to be made from used mattress material. There is a double offence involved in anything of this kind. I feel that the matter should be looked into more thoroughly. I happen to be a member of the war expenditures committee and a member of the subcommittee over which the hon. member for Bellechasse is chairman. One of the things that we have authority to go into is boards such as this one. It does seem to me in the light of the allegations that have been made to-night and the questions that have been asked that this whole matter should be gone into more thoroughly. I am a layman as far as legal matters are concerned. But I find it difficult to understand how these errors and wrongs can be made which seem to be awfully close to being fraudulent, and when the mistake is discovered all that results is that the recipient is told that he must pay back the subsidy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said a moment ago that some cases were referred to the enforcement section and that prosecutions have been taken. My hon. friend has not cited any case. If he will give me the name of any particular concern which he has in mind I shall have something to go on; I can get specific information, but when we are talking in general terms-he is talking in general terms and therefore I can only reply in general terms.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I am forced to talk in general terms by the very nature of the case. I think the parliamentary assistant should realize this. He and his minister sit
War Appropriation-Finance

there with officials in front of them and through those officials he has access to all the records. We have nothing. We are just the opposition with our bare hands, and yet it is our job to try and scrutinize every item of expenditure that is proposed in a bill such as the war appropriation bill, and try to find out if any of the public money has been wasted. I understand that a prosecution has been launched against one of the firms receiving subsidies from this corporation. I understand that that firm was manufacturing bedding. I understand that the prosecution was launched not by the corporation but by the Department of Munitions and Supply because that department found that this company was not making its bedding up to the specifications required by the department. The fact is that supposedly brand new bedding was being made out of stuff that may have been slept on for forty or fifty years. Although this may lead to a discussion that perhaps is not in order here to-night, I urge the desirability of legislation to prevent the manufacture of bedding on that basis. If the corporation is aware that a prosecution has been launched against that company because of that situation, then it seems to me that the matter has to be gone into a great deal more thoroughly, not just by inspectors of the corporation but by the Department of Finance which is responsible to parliament for these payments.
There is another aspect of the matter about which I should like to question the parliamentary assistant. I understand that the bedding administrator is an official, if not a very high one, of one of the bedding companies which receives subsidies from this corporation. What I had in mind in making that reference was this. On several occasions the Minister of Finance who I see is now in his seat, has said to the hon. member for Peterborough West, if not to others, that he did not feel it desirable to make public figures as to amounts of subsidies paid to individual corporations. He was not opposed to making public the total amount paid, but he did not wish to give the firms knowledge of the business of their competitors.
I may be wrong in this, but it does seem to me that if we have an official of one of these firms acting as the administrator, and having something to do with deciding the subsidies paid to the others, in such event we do have an unfair situation, on the basis stated by the Minister of Finance himself, namely, that of having one manufacturer knowing the conditions of his competitors, but without their knowing his. The parlia-

mentary assistant will correct me if I am wrong in drawing such an assumption from this set-up.
I should like also to know whether there have been any recoveries of subsidies from the firm from which the bedding administrator came. It does not necessarily attach anything to him personally, but I am asking if from the firm of which he was head in peace time there have been recovered any subsidies because of its being found, after investigation, that they had been wrongly paid.

War Appropriation-Finance

I think the statement the parliamentary assistant gave a few minutes ago regarding the output of farm implements is too optimistic. He is not to blame, but the fact is that these quotas are not working out as he has given them to us. There is a bottleneck somewhere. I think it is in connection with the permits. The regional controllers did not take any action on the allotments for this year until November 1 of last year. The implement distributors made their allocations on the basis of the figures they were given last November for spring operation this year. Many of the people who were entitled to and obtained permits have not been able to procure the tractors which they needed for spring seeding. Just last week I saw letters which had been received from the manufacturers stating that certain cultivators and other implements of that kind would not be manufactured until this fall.
There is a definite bottleneck somewhere and I wonder if some improvement could not be made in the method of issuing permits so that an applicant may not be misled into thinking that he will get something when in fact he cannot get it. People are complaining that when they counted on getting a tractor or some other labour saving implement for spring operations they now find that they cannot obtain it. I know many agents who had orders for drills and had obtained permits but who found that they could not obtain them until this summer, when the seeding season would be past. This has created a good deal of unnecessary confusion among the producers. I am wondering if it would not be better not to issue the permits until the machines were actually available, although the people will want to know as soon as they can if they are to be able to obtain them. If they cannot obtain them when the season comes round, it is most difficult for them. We have discussed this matter with the Minister of Munitions and Supply and he says that the steel is available. I understand that man-power is a big difficulty with respect to certain portions of the machines. I wonder if the controllers could not do something to improve the situation particularly toward supplying labour saving implements?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I will bring my hon. friend's suggestions to the attention of the minister.

Referring to the subsidy on bedding, I must say that I was shocked at the attitude of the hon. member for Winnipeg
North Centre who suspected that fraudulent charges might be laid against certain manufacturers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Some have already been laid by the enforcement officers.
We will take your word on that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the word of the parliamentary assistant.

It comes with poor grace from the hon. member who happens to be one who has deserted the pulpit to come here and supply the material needs of humanity instead of the spiritual needs. I was taught that a man with a certain weakness generally suspects other people of having the same weakness.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?
You talked for quite a while.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does he not regard this calling as an honourable one?

Yes, but I did not have to desert a more honourable one to come here. I was also shocked to think that this government sees fit to subsidize bedding, especially in war time. I have spent more time sleeping on straw ticks and mattresses than I ever spent on Beauty Rest mattresses.
I commend to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre the beautiful aroma of well threshed oat straw in a good tick. That would put him to sleep and then he would not have so many crackpot ideas to bring before the house; possibly in these times of war it would be a good thing for most of us, instead of subsidizing the manufacture of some of these things that are wasteful of labour and materials.
I am inclined to take the view in spite of all handicaps the wartime prices and trade board have done a fairly good job. Had they not come into the field and guided man's labours, we would not have accomplished as much as we have done to-day. It is a new organization and we did not have men trained in the work of distributing goods and services. They had to take in men of no great experience. But in the main the board has done a good job. I feel that we spend too much time in pointing out little irregularities here and there to this thing and that, when we could be utilizing our energies to much better advantage.

Agreed.
War Appropriation-Finance

Take the group represented by my hon. friend, and you will see that they have filled up more columns of Hansard this session than any other group in the house. I do not say that to be unkind, but I was just wondering why they feel it necessary to spend so much time in giving us the benefit of the work of their analytical minds. They seem to know how to go about it. I must say that I have not as suspicious a mind as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has. I believe that the great majority of the people of the country want to play the game and want to play it fair. There is the odd man who is unpatriotic and who will bootleg a little gasoline or something like that, but society frowns down upon ihat sort of thing and the wrongdoer knows it. I am just trying to state things as I see them in my own quiet way, as I sit here wondering why we spend so much time in discussing some very small things, thereby delaying the business of the house.

There is one side to this vote that, so far as I know, has not been mentioned by any one. The purpose of the vote has been to control prices and perhaps to increase production in certain lines in the interests of the prosecution of the war and the welfare of the people at large. There are about two hundred items in these war appropriation estimates, and this vote of $140,000,000 is about the sixth or seventh largest of the votes. Has any tabulation been made showing how much money has been saved to the country by a vote of this kind? That is what interests me more than anything else. The vote was originated for the very real purpose of controlling prices, preventing inflation, and perhaps increasing business in some lines. But nothing has been said as yet by the parliamentary assistant to show just what the country has been saving through the operation of the wartime prices and trade board. We might be able to find fault with scores of individual things that are done, but what interests me is the large results that have been obtained by the operations of the board. I would like the parliamentary assistant to rise in his place and say that this vote of $140,000,000, the vote of $120,000,000 last year and similar votes in other years have saved this country, let us say, one billion dollars through preventing inflation, and let him give a break-down showing just how the money has been saved.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is a little difficult to give any concrete estimate of what has been saved. As the hon. member for Davenport has pointed out, the purpose of consumer subsidies is to

enable essential goods to be sold at ceiling prices instead of allowing prices to rise, because obviously if prices of some essential goods rise, prices of others will go up and you will have a more or less general price rise. It is considered that by the use of selective subsidies on essential consumer goods, which in effect means that the increased cost of these things is spread over the people as a whole by taxation, you avoid a general rise in the cost of living. It is estimated-these figures have been given either by the minister or by Mr. Donald Gordon-that a one point rise in the cost of living means an additional expenditure by the Canadian people of some $35,000,000 a year. Therefore the expenditure of $140,000,000, which is the estimate for this year-it was less than that last year-in consumer subsidies is the equivalent of approximately a four point general rise in the cost of living. Those competent to judge consider that without the payment of these subsidies the rise in the cost of living would have been greatly in excess of four points. We are always comparing this war with the last war, when we did not have a system of price control and did not use subsidies, as has been the case here. At the period of the last war which corresponds with the end of 1943 the cost of living had risen fifty-six points, as against a rise at the end of 1943 of 18-2 or 18-3.

And each point, you
said, amounts to about $35 millions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Each point rise in the cost of living, it is estimated, means an increased cost to the people of Canada of $35 million a year.

On that basis there has
been a very great saving?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes. I am not suggesting
that the subsidies account for that entire saving, but they are part of the over-all programme of price, wage and salary control, together with the fiscal programme of heavy taxation and periodical victory loans; they are all part of the picture, and it is felt that they play an essential part in maintaining a stable level of prices. It is pointed out to me that the government is spending nearly $5,000 million a year, and that if prices went up, let us say tea per cent, the government costs would go up perhaps $250 million, which would have to be raised by taxation, or borrowing, or both.

I believe I can give the parliamentary assistant one commodity on which definite figures could be obtained. I remember clearly a period in the last war

War Appropriation-Finance
when the price of anthracite coal advanced from about $14.50 to $21, a difference of $6.50. During this war the price has risen to some extent, but nowhere near the height it reached during the last war. I imagine that if the department is able to obtain the approximate number of tons of anthracite coal burned in Canada throughout the year, and multiplies it by the difference of $6.50 a ton, it would have some figure to show what has been saved. The Canadian people want to believe that, through the expenditure of $140 million on this vote to control prices, bonuses and so forth, the country saves infinitely more. The parliamentary assistant has given some figures in proof of that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I think that can be safely
asserted.

Perhaps before he finishes he may have other definite figures, which would dispose the public to accept this expenditure. Here are we, the opposition, letting through-not that we could stop it if we wanted, to, but without too much opposition, or indeed without any opposition, and not much inquiry-a vote of $140 million. The public look to us to bring out the reasons for so large a vote. If it can be shown, as the parliamentary assistant has done in part, that an expenditure of $140 million will save $1,500 million or $2,000 million, there would be no opposition to it in the country, and of course His Majesty's loyal opposition would not be blamed too much for having let the vote go through so easily.

When the house rose
on Tuesday night I asked the parliamentary assistant if he would give us a more detailed statement with respect to the operations of the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation. Since that time I have had an opportunity of reading through the report of the wartime prices and trade board, and I wish to compliment that body on being, I believe, the only one which has given us information of an authentic character right up to December 31, 1943. Most of the questions which I intended to ask the parliamentary assistant have been quite satisfactorily answered in this report. The parliamentary assistant has broken down to some extent the $140 million item. He told us that domestic and other subsidies would amount to about $115,500,000. I should like to have had the specific amounts paid for imports, particularly general imports. He gave us a break-down of the domestic subsidies. I thought the expression which he used, namely, "losses," was unfortunate, because it conveys a peculiar idea to the general
public. In reality it is not a loss; it is a subsidy paid by that particular branch of the corporation on that particular item.
For a moment I turn to page 25 of the report, which deals with potatoes. It is stated, "To encourage the movement of potatoes from Saskatchewan and Manitoba to northern Ontario and the northwestern part of Quebec a subsidy was paid covering the extra transportation costs involved." I wonder why mention there is made of only two of the western provinces, namely Saskatchewan and Manitoba. Although there was a tremendous crop of potatoes in Alberta, there is no reference to the fact that any potatoes have been shipped east from Alberta or any subsidy paid. The amount of transportation subsidy was a little more than $15,000 on the old crop of potatoes and a little more on the 1943 crop.
I had a number of other questions, but I shall not delay the committee. The only other question I desire to ask has to do with a subsidy paid on horsehair. I received a letter from one of my constituents, and when I read it I must confess that I laughed because I thought it was rather a ridiculous request to ask me to explain something on the subject which appeared in one of the western newspapers. The report in the west was to the effect that the prices board were anxious to get a large quantity of horsehair, and that if the domestic supply did not come forward in sufficient volume to take care of the needs of the armed forces and the war plants it would be necessary to import horsehair from South America. Upon looking up the auditor general's report, in which the figures given are no later than March 31, 1943 -perhaps the parliamentary assistant could bring them up to the end of March, 1944- I find that the amount of horsehair purchased for use in Canada cost $653,370. That astonished me. It was sold to the trade, I assume, for $677,315, or a profit on the deal of $23,945. The part of the article that I do not understand is this. The price of good quality horsehair ranges from thirty cents to fifty cents a pound, and any wool and hide dealer will buy it. There must be a reasonable answer for that statement as to why in the domestic market the producer should receive only from thirty to fifty cents a pound, whereas the material imported from South America was able to command a price of $2 a pound. These are the two items.
I might also ask the parliamentary assistant to give me some idea as to the deal which was made between the corporation and the banks with respect to the charges made by them connected with milk subsidies. I un-

derstand that a substantial sum of money was paid to the banking institutions for work in connection with subsidies covering milk, and I should like to have an explanation of that particular item. I would ask the parliamentary assistant also to bring up to date the statement which is to be found at the bottom of page 64, appendix 1, where it gives the actual expenditures from April 1, 1943, to December 31, 1943. Will he bring that up to the end of March, 1944, and give a breakdown of the two items, including local ration board? speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
First I wish to thank my
hon. friend for his complimentary reference to the report of the wartime prices and trade board. I agree that it is a good report. It was made for the nine-month period in order that we might table it reasonably early in the session. Hon. members will recall that it was tabled early in February. Last year the report was for the full period up to March 31, but unfortunately we could not get it in until the latter part of May or early in June. We felt this year that it would be useful if it were tabled earlier. Now the figures are available for the first twelvemonth period, and I shall be glad, as my hon. friend has suggested, to bring the figures up to date. I do not know if the statements here should be printed in Hansard. We do not want to make a fresh report. The figures with respect to subsidy payments cover the nine-month period up to December 31. We have now the figures for the subsequent three months, so that it will be possible for us to place on Hansard a statement showing the payments for the full twelve-month period, and similarly a statement can be given of the actual expenditures of the wartime prices and trade board for the full period, although, as my hon. friend will appreciate, that does not relate to the item we are now considering. It is the item of $15,600,000, passed on Tuesday. Perhaps it would serve the purpose af the committee if I were to table a statement of the actual expenditures of the prices board for the twelve-month period. It would be available to any member who wanted it.
Can the parliamentary assistant give the reason-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The hon. member asked
about the subsidy on potatoes. I am informed that at the time of the great scarcity last May, the only place in Canada where there were surplus potatoes was in Saskatchewan. There may have been a car or two in Mani-

toba, but not many. What was done in effect was to pay a transportation subsidy on these potatoes, which were the only surplus potatoes available, to bring them to eastern Canada.
On the question of horsehair, I understand that is an essential material. Formerly the bristles used in brushes came to us from China, but that source has been cut off, and consequently we have had to rely on domestic horsehair and such hair as could be obtained from abroad. We are not now importing any. We are able to get it from domestic supplies, but it is bulk-purchased by the corporation and made available to brush manufacturers. Brushes are required for paint work in connection with various war industries.
When was the importation of horsehair discontinued?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am not sure that we have that information. It is subject to import permit and is ineligible for subsidy. No subsidy has ever been paid on imported horsehair.

I understand that the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation was set up as a company under the Companies Act. The corporation was empowered to carry on the duties and responsibilities through incorporation and organization of subsidiary companies, and one at least has been set up under the terms of that order in council, one known as the Wartime Food Corporation Limited. Is that the only one, or are there others?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is the only subsidiary of Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation.
Can the parliamentary assistant give a short resume of the operations of that corporation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Wartime Food Corporation is a subsidiary of Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation and it operated in the live cattle market for a time during 1942. It was inactive during 1943 and began renewed operations on a reorganized basis, including representation on its board of directors for both primary producers and organized labour in January of this year, 1944. It was reorganized for the purpose of ensuring that supplies of fresh fruits and vegetables were available in Canada and equitably distributed -empowered to bulk purchase or otherwise deal in fresh fruits and vegetables, both domestic and imported if necessary.
One of the first responsibilities of the Wartime Food Corporation was to assume

War Appropriation-Finance
control of distribution of potatoes in eastern Canada-I hope we do not start the potato argument again-in order to ensure supplies for deficiency areas and to meet the requirements of the armed forces and other preferred users. In addition to controlling distribution, Wartime Food Corporation bulk purchased potatoes both from British Columbia and later from Maine.
Under authorization from wartime prices and trade board Wartime Food Corporation has also paid a root vegetable freight subsidy covering potatoes, cabbages, carrots and parsnips. Wartime Foods now pays subsidies on potato freight eastern and on oranges imported from the United States of America, both formerly paid by Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation; but that is purely for reasons of internal economy.
Who is at the head of Wartime Foods Corporation, the same individuals?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
The directors are set out in the report which my hon. friend has in front of him. The president is R. T. Mohan; vicepresident K. W. Taylor who is sitting in front of me; general manager, J. B. Lander; secretary-treasurer, H. N. H. James. The directors are: A. R. Johnstone, S. R. Noble, E. W. Smart, Raoul Godbout and Carl Sanders.
The break-down of the estimates for 194445 is as follows: There is provision for potential subsidy on potatoes of $750,000, a similar payment with respect to oranges of $2,000,000; cost of administration, $75,000, and miscellaneous, $175,000, making up the total estimate of $3,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Wartime Food Corporation has been mentioned. I wish to refer to the Wartime Food Corporation in the earlier phase of its activity, when it was not dealing with fruits and vegetables at all but was responsible for the market support of cattle prices. I wish to deal with one phase and one phase only. In a debate which took place under another item on May 23, 1944, Mr. Donald Gordon's name was mentionel several times by the hon. member for Lethbridge. The references to Mr. Donald Gordon were such as these. On page 3175 of Hansard at the bottom of column 1, Mr. Gordon's name is used and a press release which was issued on October 7, 1942, was quoted. In the first column on page 3176 reference is made to an undertaking contained in a press release by Donald Gordon to purchase any surpluses of beef to meet shifts in the price. In the first column of page 3177 reference is made to a promise in Donald Gordon's press release.
In a sense I am speaking on behalf of Mr. Gordon now. He is extremely jealous of his reputation for honour in carrying out his commitments, and I want to make clear that so long as the wartime prices and trade board was responsible for the operations referred to in the press release of October 7, 1942, those commitments were scrupulously carried out. During the period from June 28 to August 17, 1942, 49,727 head of cattle were purchased and 1,524 were exported to the United States. In this operation a loss of $832,281.69 was incurred. The board stood ready throughout to continue the support if surplus supply had threatened to depress cattle prices unduly. On May 21, 1943, however, an announcement was made and widely publicized in the form of a joint statement issued by the Department of Agriculture and the wartime prices and trade board, with the approval of the government, in which it was made clear that the support of the market from then on would not be the responsibility of the wartime prices and trade board. My colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, made it clear in the house that the responsibility as from that date, namely, the spring of 1943, was assumed by the meat board. That reference is found near the bottom of the second column of page 3177 of Hansard.
' It may be that a complete reading of the debate found in the columns to which I have referred makes it perfectly clear that there was no violation of commitments on the part of Mr. Gordon or the wartime prices and trade board or the Wartime Food Corporation. It may be that is perfectly clear already, but since there were several references to a promise made by Donald Gordon personally and a violation of that promise I thought I owed it to Mr. Gordon-and I know he would like me to make this clear to the committee-to say that there was no violation or breach of any commitment whatever on their part, and I have no reason to think there was any on the part of the meat board either, I may say.

There is an item or two on which I should like to make some representations to the senior officials of the Department of Finance and the officials of the wartime prices and trade board respecting subsidies. But before doing so I wish to add a word of appreciation to those already spoken by the hon. member for New Westminster and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance respecting the work which has been so well done by those who have volunteered to distribute ration books. This group of un-
War Appropriation-Finance

selfish and untiring citizens is deserving of the highest commendation by the government and the people of Canada.
Something has been said in this discussion this evening with regard to the value to the Canadian people of the work which has been done by the wartime prices and trade board. It would be a long story to cover all the items in which I think the people of Canada generally have been well served by this board, but I wish to point out two items. I refer to sugar and automobile tires. Those are items in which the supply is not sufficient to meet the demand, and if it were not for the control and the rationing of those commodities I am quite satisfied that the extra cost of those two items would run into many millions of dollars which would have to be paid by the general public. Therefore I think we should give credit where credit is due and highly commend the minister and those associated with him in this most essential and worth-while part of the war effort of the Canadian people.
If I had any criticism of the administration of these matters by the wartime prices and trade board it would be this. I am not sure that the officials throughout the Dominion of Canada who are in charge of these regional offices are always as considerate and as courteous to the public as they should be. I do not think it would be at all amiss if these officials were brought in at least once a year to some central point, so that the higher officials in the department could give them some instructions. They might be told that while we have to enforce restrictions, they should be enforced in a manner which would not be offensive to the general public.
I now come to one or two items concerning which I wish to make some representations. The first has to do with clover seed. I believe there are some lines of clover seed for which the grower is not receiving sufficient remuneration, so as to encourage production. To my mind this production is essential not only during the war, but in the post-war period. We have enjoyed for many years a substantial share of the import markets in Europe for clover seed. I believe that, particularly with respect to alsike seed, the present price is not sufficient to give that impetus which is so necessary to the maintenance of production on a large scale.
I believe members of the committee generally will agree with me when I say that very large quantities of seed will be required in Europe when the war is over. Therefore, if we are to be in a position to supply and to retain that substantial market, I think some consideration should be given to the possibility of

paying a subsidy on at least some of these lines. The prices, as I recall them, are these: For alsike seed, twenty-nine cents a pound; for red clover, thirty-four cents a pound and for alfalfa seed, thirty-seven cents a pound. That is the price at which the dealer is permitted to sell to the retail trade in Canada. Perhaps those are reasonable prices for the consumer in Canada to pay.
Of course, so far as exports are concerned, the seed business of Canada is controlled by the export seed office, which is located in the town of Lindsay, in my riding. The official in charge of the export seed office, under the direction of the seed branch, is Mr. F. G. Perrin, general manager of the Hogg and Lytle Seed Company, a man who has had a wide trading experience in both domestic and export seed markets. I state that only to illustrate that the area I represent is a large clover seed producing district, particularly so far as alsike and red clover seeds are concerned.
I think the official returns will show this year that the alfalfa seed growers have received a fair price. I am not sure, however, that that is the case with respect to alsike. Of course the seed is turned over to the export office by the seed dealers at a price which is substantially lower than the retail domestic price to which I have referred. Then the grower is entitled, through participation certificates, to receive whatever additional sum may represent the profit on the export trade. I believe that is a sound set-up, because under other circumstances the dealers would profit to a greater extent.
We now come back to the price of alsike seed. A good deal of the seed was brought in at $10 a bushel. Some seed dealers at a later time paid an additional $2.50 a bushel. But even at that the returns to the grower are not sufficient to give that encouragement which is so necessary if we are to produce substantial quantities of seed. If we had enjoyed a heavy export for the 1943 crop of alsike the situation would have been more satisfactory from the point of view of the grower, because there would have been returned to him by the export seed office a substantial payment by way of participation certificates. That, however, was not the case. Our exports of alsike seed from the 1943 crop were practically negligible, so that there cannot be any substantial sum returned to the growers.
It is true that if the price at which the dealers must turn the seed over to the export office were increased, it would mean that the seed trade could go out and buy the seed from the growers at a higher price. The final result might not be very much different

War Appropriation

Finance
from what it is under the present set-up, but the grower would receive a larger down payment, and to that extent would be that much better satisfied. It is a long time to look ahead to what may come from a participation certificate. That applies particularly to the class of producers who have not been accustomed to receiving returns from those certificates.
It is my considered opinion with respect to alsike that a subsidy of 7 or 7i cents a pound would give that encouragement so essential to maintain production on a scale which will provide ample seed, so that we may retain our share of that important European market during the war, and in the post-war period. I would ask the responsible officials to give most serious consideration to the possibility of putting into effect a subsidy of about those proportions in respect of alsike seed.
Then, some little additional encouragement would not be out of line in respect of red clover seed. Where red clover seed is produced we always find a good crop of hay. At least I can say it is usual to find that where you have a good crop of seed you have at least a fair crop of hay. In that way the grower has the advantage of two crops in one year. That does not pertain to alsike seed. After the threshing the feed is of very little value, and alsike clover seed is produced entirely from the first crop.
Alfalfa seed is not produced in large quantities in my community. However, substantial quantities of that seed are produced from a second crop. So that in that instance, too, the grower in many instances has a crop of hay, and then he can produce his seed from his second crop. It is also true that large quantities of alfalfa seed are produced in western Canada, and in some portions of Ontario, from the first cutting.
There is one further item to which I should like to make a brief reference, namely, Ontario fall wheat. There is a ceiling price on Ontario fall wheat of approximately $1.26 a bushel at Montreal, which nets the On'ario grower anywhere from $1.10 to $1.12 a bushel. My understanding is, although I may be mistaken, that there is no ceiling on western wheat. At the present time the price of Ontario wheat is below that of western wheat. That may not pertain right back to the grower, but in ordinary times Ontario fall wheat is sold at from ten to twenty cents above No. 1 northern. The result has been and will continue to be that a large portion of the Ontario fall wheat crop will go into the feed bin. Over a long period of years
we have built up and developed a profitable and substantial business in pastry flour which is produced from Ontario fall wheat.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me to interrupt? I do not want to stop him, but this question of Ontario wheat really comes under a later item in these estimates. I do not know whether he would prefer to discuss it now or later on.
I was going to suggest that if the price ceiling cannot be altered consideration be given to the payment of a subsidy.
The first question I should like to ask the Minister of Finance is whether I should call his assistant the parliamentary assistant or secretary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I believe the official title is parliamentary assistant.

I should like to revert to the broom corn industry and ask the parliamentary assistant if the government had anything to do with financing or promoting certain companies which bargained with quite a number of farmers in some sections of the country to grow broom corn? In many cases the broom corn was never harvested because the contracts were misleading and it was found that the remuneration to be received was not sufficient to pay the labour involved in the harvesting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I am advised that the government had nothing to do with organizing or promoting the companies to which my hon. friend has referred. Perhaps I had better restrict my statement to the wartime prices and trade board or the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, whose estimates we are now discussing. They had nothing to do with the promotion of any such companies. I have no information about other departments of the government, but I am inclined to doubt that they had anything to do with it.

I appreciate the great care the Minister of Finance took in framing his statement in defence of Mr. Gordon. I was involved in the attack on the government which involved Mr. Gordon, but I think a careful perusal of the remarks I made will show that I did not directly attach blame to Mr. Gordon. I think I made it quite clear that I did not know who was to blame, that the object of my remarks was to find out where the blame should be placed. Since it has been made clear by the statement of the minister that Mr. Gordon had control until the spring of 1943-what month was it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
May 21.
War Appropriation -Finance

That statement certainly exonerates Mr. Gordon and will raise him to a high regard of esteem in my constituency because there were no complaints before that date. What I said was based on what happened in 1044, and I think the minister recognizes that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not saying that there may be any blame.

I am not saying that there should be any blame attached to Mr. Gordon, but certainly there is plenty attached to whoever took over from that time. However, we are not discussing this matter at the present time, so that I shall not go into it in any detail. I just wanted to make it clear that I did not wisih to make an unjustified attack on Mr. Gordon. As a matter of fact, I was just trying to find out who was to blame so that I would know whom to shoot at. I am glad one of them is eliminated. All through the months of February and March the impression was abroad in my constituency that somehow or another the wartime prices and trade board was responsible, or at least partly responsible. It will be remembered from what I said that one of our great difficulties has been that we do not know upon whom to place the blame. It would now appear that the blame is entirely on the Minister of Agriculture. I am afraid I gave the minister the benefit of the doubt, but in my next speech I will not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am very sorry if my remarks were taken as an attempt to shift the blame, because really I did not say any more than the Minister of Agriculture said himself.
He is reported on page 3177 of Hansard as follows:
Mr. Gardiner: My hon. friend has read the statement and I now say to him that that particular arrangement was changed.
Mr. Blackmore: When was it changed?
Mr. Gardiner: It wyas changed in the spring >f 1943.	*	K
Mr. Blackmore: From that time thereafter-[DOT] Mr. Gardiner: From the time the meat board was set up it became responsible for purchasing meat.

That was a good thing for the Minister of Agriculture to say. The trouble was that whoever tried to probe into the matter to determine wherein the responsibility lay always found that the wartime prices and trade board turned up. That has been where the difficulty lay. I believe that my attack was justified, but I am happy to know that Mr. Gordon is out of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
A matter was raised earlier ihis evening by the hon. member for Belle-
[Mr. Ilsley.J
chasse who is not in his seat at the moment. I did not have the information at the time he inquired about tobacco prices. I am advised that the matter has been under consideration for some little time and that a decision will probably be given within the course of the next few days.

Last week I referred to the subsidy which was paid by the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation to the producers of pit props and mine ties in western Canada. It was pointed out to me at the time that this matter did not properly come under the estimates of the Minister of Mines and Resources. It will be recalled that in 1943 a serious shortage of these items developed, and it was decided by the wartime prices and trade board that the mine operators could not stand an increase in price. It was also understood that a drop in the production of pit props and mine ties resulted because the producers were unable to procure help or to pay the wages demanded. Therefore the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation was authorized to pay a subsidy of $3.50 per thousand lineal feet on pit props and something like one-half cent per foot for mine ties. This continued until February, 1944, and I am not complaining because it was paid.
What I complain about is this, that without notice the subsidy was terminated. Our producers had in their yards thousands of lineal feet of pit props and mine ties. They had paid wages on the understanding that the subsidy would be continued. When it was suddenly discontinued they found themselves in a most unfortunate predicament. It was true they were told that they might increase the price of their product by $3.50 a thousand, and in the case of mine ties by the amount of the subsidy. But for two reasons they discovered that there was no market for their pit props and mine ties, one reason being that we now have a surplus. The second reason I am not going to press because some of the ministers take exception to this. The operator said, "He can buy the government produced commodity more cheaply than we can buy yours." But I am not going to press that.
I should like to know why the subsidy was discontinued. Was it because the mine operators were not in a position to pay the additional price? Could it be that the subsidy was discontinued because of there now being a surplus? I should like to get to the bottom of this. I am much opposed to this idea of getting operators to cooperate through a subsidy and then penalizing them for their cooperation., and that is exactly what this

War Appropriation-Finance
amounted to. They met your shortage; they had a surplus; you discontinued the subsidy; they were caught.
The situation is this. The labour shortage is undoubtedly going to get worse. Another winter might be very severe. Then it is reasonable to expect that another shortage of these very necessary commodities will develop. Can you expect the operators to cooperate as they did before? I think an important principle is involved. I would ask the parliamentary assistant to give me the reason for the discontinuation of the payment of that subsidy, at least on the materials which were in the yards and had been purchased with the idea that the subsidy would be paid.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The reason is that the subsidy was superseded by price increases which were equal to the amounts to be allowed to producers of pit props and mine ties, effective from January 19, 1944.

I referred to that. But the point is this, that a surplus had been created. Then, of course, we know that prisoners of war and conscientious objectors had also been engaged in the production of these commodities. When the operators increased their prices by $3.50 there was no market for them. The assumption was, and it is based on the statement of the operators: "We can buy them from' the government more cheaply." But I am not going to press that. The Minister of Labour denied that although I could have produced enough evidence to convince him that I had a case, but my object was not to try to make a case. There is an important principle involved, and we may desire the cooperation of these people later on.

Has consideration been given to avoiding in some way or another the difficulties that some producers get themselves into as a result of the fixing of a ceiling price which gradually rises to a higher point? We have a situation in our community with respect to potatoes. We produce potatoes quite extensively, but our potatoes are not graded. We can grow good potatoes, but there has never been set up in the community the machinery necessary for the grading of potatoes. That makes it difficult to market our potatoes outside the local neighbourhood or the local towns.
What happened this year was that numbers of farmers who have potatoes, some hundreds of bags, stored them, believing that they would get the spring ceiling price. They probably could have sold them last fall or found a market for them during the winter months,
but they wanted to hold for the spring ceiling price. Then a shortage of potatoes developed, and potatoes were brought in from British Columbia and some from the United States to supply the market. The result is that numbers of farmers in my community have hundreds of bags of potatoes on their hands for which they cannot find a market. It looks to me as though something ought to be done to prevent the encouragement of that sort of thing. It is quite easy to say that the farmer has himself to blame, that he should have sold when he could have got a reasonable price. But most people like to get the top price. It is difficult to market potatoes in our climate in the winter months, and it is not easy to ship potatoes out of our community in carload lots for the reason that they are not graded. It is not easy to sell a carload of potatoes in the city of Ottawa, unless they are graded. The markets we used to have for potatoes was with the truckers who would run up from Ottawa, perhaps with a load, and take back a load of potatoes. But now these trucks cannot go beyond the thirty-five mile limit, and our neighbourhood trucks are not allowed to truck potatoes into the city of Ottawa, 100 miles away. The way it looks now, these potatoes are going to be a total loss. A repetition of that sort of situation should be guarded against. I would ask the parliamentary assistant if the officials could somehow get their heads together and find a market for the potatoes of these grievously disappointed farmers in my community.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have listened with interest to the hon. member for Renfrew North and I am getting quite a liberal education in potatoes. I will bring his remarks to the attention of the officials and ask them whether anything can be done.

I called the board's attention to the question mentioned by the previous speaker in February and March before they started to import potatoes. The War Foods Corporation said: We will import potatoes from the United States. They failed to take my advice. They imported some two hundred and fifty carloads. I will say that the War Foods Corporation did a much better job than the Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation, because they bought the potatoes from the war food distributing board in the United States, and they bought them away below our ceiling and saved the payment of any subsidy.
I see by this report that $1,300,000 was paid in subsidies on corn. Was that domestic or imported com? Was the corn used for feeding purposes or for processing into com starch, glucose and corn syrup?
War Appropriation-Finance

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It was all imported com, and I understand that it was largely used for corn starch and corn meal.

In spite of the efforts which have been made to control prices, I am informed that manufacturers of lumber are receiving more for their lumber than they did in the last war. I notice that a subsidy in the form of a ten per cent discount is paid the final consumer in certain cases. Final consumers who are eligible for the discount are " farmers, fishermen, growers of fruit and vegetables, trappers and other civilian users who purchase lumber from time to time for use in the pursuit of their personal trade or occupation, for maintenance and repair purposes, or for use in assisting the primary production of essential foods." We hear a great deal about the necessity for new dwellings; and the people who own and occupy houses have to make necessary repairs to them from time to time. In view of the increased cost of lumber these' repairs add to their cost of living; and I ask the parliamentary assistant if any consideration has ever been given to the question of including owners of houses to provide that they obtain this discount.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Repairs are eligible, not new construction.
Repairs to houses are eligible?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: So I am advised, yes.
As I read page 34 of the report of the wartime prices and trade board, it does not say that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That may have been an oversight.
In fact it says, " The subsidy is not paid on sales to industrial users and contractors and on lumber for the building or improvement of dwellings."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: That is right-on new building and improvements, but that does not cover repairs. Repairs and maintenance are included, not new building or improvements to existing buildings; and not, of course, for industrial uses.

In regard to lumber, the parliamentary assistant told us there was a certain amount in this item for subsidy. Could he tell us how much the price ceiling on lumber has been lifted since the basic period of 1940?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I may not have that information. Some price advances have been authorized, and they have varied in different regions of the country. I am afraid I have not the information here, nor have I any average figure here.

Possibly the parliamentary assistant could get that. I believe that the ceiling on lumber has been raised several times in some sections of the country, and I should like to know, if it is possible to get the information, by what percentage it has been raised since the basic period.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
I will try to get that
information.
Does that subsidy on lumber include all grades, or is there any specified grade?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: It is payable on all classes of lumber, but not on sashes, doors, millwork and so on; and only on soft wood lumber, not on hardwoods.
Is there a subsidy on raw and refined sugar?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: No.
